# Part XII: Practice and Operations {#part-practice .unnumbered}

> "A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple
> system that works."
>
> John Gall, ["Systemantics"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systemantics)

The last substantive part moves from explaining mechanisms to operating them.
Part IX went below the model to accelerators, compilers, power, and failure at
scale. Part X took up the limits that remain once hardware is granted: the finite
stock of learnable signal, the measurement of progress, and the cost of
verifying a result. Part XI examined the terms under which the stack is supplied
and used, from model releases and prices to market structure, adoption, and data
rights. This part asks how a team should wire the stack together and run it in
production. Its chapters apply the earlier mechanisms to choices made under
deadlines, budgets, licenses, reliability targets, changing model releases, and
production incidents.

@sec-choosing-model starts from a workload contract and compares versioned
served systems against it, whether hosted or self-hosted: eligibility gates
first, then a paired evaluation on the workload, cost per accepted task, and a
recorded trade-off. @sec-serving-stack, @sec-edge, and @sec-training-practice
carry the chosen system into serving engines, gateways, and compute, into
on-device deployment, and into fine-tuning when a behavior has to live in the
weights. @sec-agents-practice and @sec-retrieval-practice bring in agent
frameworks, sandboxes, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool calls, coding
agents, document parsing, authorized retrieval, and extraction.
@sec-eval-practice binds evaluation and trace evidence to the exact system
released, and @sec-wiring-stack composes the components through boundary
contracts, a reference architecture, and accounting for the accepted task.
@sec-deployment-lifecycle, @sec-reliability, @sec-human-interface-oversight,
@sec-data-engine, and @sec-operating-contracts then cover operation after
release: promotion and recovery, reliability for nondeterministic outcomes,
human review and approval gates, production data, SLOs, cost governance,
incidents, multi-tenancy, and the path that turns a production failure into a
qualified test.

The chapters read a production AI system as a set of versioned contracts, each
a written statement of what must hold, how it is measured, and where it is
enforced. The contracts record which model revision is pinned, which budget is
enforced, and which data is trusted. They say where execution is contained,
which tenant boundary is protected, and which side effects need human approval.
They name the evaluation that can block a release, and they describe how an
incident record changes the system and how a failure becomes a regression test.
Each contract also carries its re-evaluation triggers and expiry, because
models, prices, and workloads keep changing after the first release. A team can
operate, change, and recover the assembled stack to the extent that these
contracts are written down, versioned, and tested.
